explanation: The melody is an older French song, 'Ah vous dirai-je, maman', already in print when Mozart was a small child. He later wrote twelve piano variations on it.

claims.text: Mozart did not compose the melody of Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.
The melody of Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star is that of the French song Ah vous dirai-je, maman.
Ah vous dirai-je, maman was in print by 1761, when Mozart was a small child.
Mozart wrote twelve variations for piano on Ah vous dirai-je, maman.

writerNotes: Self-check (§9.3). Lint: clean under content:check for writer w-pmusic01w. Claims: every checkable statement in the stem, options and explanation is listed, with risk at or above the C26 floor and raised where a fact is beyond everyday knowledge; c1 is high because the item is counterintuitive (the C26 floor), and since the schema's riskReason list has no counterintuitive value it carries checker_doubt. Datasets: no pinned dataset covers these music facts (the manifest holds geographic, scientific, Nobel, Olympic and art-collection data), so each high-risk claim needs web evidence from the checkers. I used no WebSearch. Rival test: argued for 'true': Mozart's variations on the tune are famous and often played to children, which is how the myth spreads; the tune was printed by 1761, when he was five, so he did not compose it. The answer is false (tfKind myth). Volatility: evergreen; no time words, and nothing depends on knowledge newer than mid-2026. Regional: the tune is sung worldwide (it is also the alphabet song), and the myth is common in many countries. Style: Oxford spelling, straight quotes, no en or em dashes, explanation within 35 words. Myths: screened against myths.json, no hit; this myth is not in the list yet, so I suggest the editor adds it. Mystery: not applicable to a practice item. Encore: not applicable to a practice item. Doubts: None of substance; the French tune's earlier printing is well documented.
